question.:question/problem: Consider the function $g(x, y) = \frac{4x^{2}}{y}$. What is the rate of change of $g(x, y)$ at the point $(3, 4)$ in the direction of the vector $v = ⟨ -1, 2⟩$?
question.:question/worked-solution:
The rate of change of $g(x,y)$ at the point $(3, 4)$ in the direction of $v$ is equal to the directional derivative ${g}_{u}^{′}(3, 4).$

First, we find the unit vector $u$ in the direction of $v:$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖ & =\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+{2}^{2}}=\sqrt{5} \\ u & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}⟨-1,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the gradient $∇g(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(3, 4):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇g(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{4x^{2}}{y}),\,\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{4x^{2}}{y})⟩ \\ & =⟨\frac{8x}{y},\,-\frac{4x^{2}}{y^{2}}⟩ \\ ∇g(3, 4) & =⟨\frac{4\cdot 2\cdot 3}{4},\,-\frac{4\cdot {3}^{2}}{{4}^{2}}⟩ \\ & =⟨6,-\frac{9}{4}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the directional derivative ${g}_{u}^{′}(3, 4)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}_{u}^{′}(3, 4) & =∇g(3, 4)\cdot u \\ & =⟨6,-\frac{9}{4}⟩\cdot ⟨-\frac{\sqrt{5}}{5},\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{5}⟩ \\ & =\frac{6\cdot (-1)+(-\frac{9}{4})\cdot 2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ & =-\frac{21\sqrt{5}}{10}.\end{aligned}
